title: Trauma primary survey (ATLS)
subject: surgery
summary: Order the ABCDE by what kills fastest, and treat the chest, shock and fluid traps the exam sets.

objectives.text: Pick the first step in the primary survey and put ABCDE in order by speed of killing, not by visibility
Decide what to do next for a patient who is talking, and when to repeat the airway check; pick GCS 8 or less as the trigger for a definitive airway
Choose the emergency surgical airway for an adult versus a child under 12
Treat tension pneumothorax at once by clinical diagnosis, with needle decompression before X-ray or ventilation, at the site the exam expects
Tell tension pneumothorax from massive haemothorax and cardiac tamponade by neck veins, percussion, trachea and Beck's triad
Recognise the early sign of haemorrhagic shock, the class where hypotension appears, and the cases that mislead (neurogenic, child, elderly, beta-blocker)
Choose the initial fluid volume and type, and the target in brain injury versus haemorrhage
Send an unstable patient to FAST not CT, and pick the urethrogram before catheterisation
State that the secondary survey and AMPLE history begin only after the primary survey and resuscitation
Give the antifibrinolytic and its time window in bleeding trauma
Name the three peaks of trauma death and the one ATLS targets

traps.trap: Haemorrhage is the leading preventable death, so control bleeding before securing the airway (also absorbs TR13: xABCDE / MARCH order carried into an ATLS question)
A patient who talks is fully safe, so the primary survey can stop there
Tension pneumothorax needs a chest X-ray before decompression
An unstable trauma patient goes to CT for abdominal bleeding (also absorbs TR24: FAST treated as confirming organ injury)
Ventilate or intubate the tension pneumothorax patient before decompressing
Hypotension with bradycardia in trauma is haemorrhagic shock
Tension pneumothorax and massive haemothorax look the same on examination
Beck's triad belongs to tension pneumothorax
Hypotension appears early in haemorrhage (Class II)
Initial crystalloid bolus is 2 L in adults (old PYQ key; Ringer-lactate-only variant TR12 handled in feedback)
Needle decompression goes in the 2nd intercostal space, mid-clavicular line, in adults
Paradoxical chest-wall movement causes the hypoxia in flail chest
Tracheal deviation points toward the injured side in tension pneumothorax
Normal vital signs exclude shock in children, the elderly, pregnancy and beta-blocked patients
Surgical cricothyroidotomy is the emergency airway for a child
Insert a urinary catheter first to check for urethral injury
The third peak (sepsis, days to weeks) is the window ATLS targets
A chest injury list for the primary survey is any chest injury, including simple pneumothorax and rib fractures, with tamponade left out
Permissive hypotension is the target in traumatic brain injury
Tranexamic acid works up to 8 hours

segments.title: Why the order, and when do patients die

say.text: Before we teach anything, let's see what you already carry.
A road-accident victim is wheeled in with a spurting thigh wound. What is the first priority in the **primary survey** of Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS)?

choices.label: Tourniquet on the bleeding thigh wound
Airway, with the neck held still
Two large-bore IV lines with warm fluid
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which problem would end this patient in minutes if nobody dealt with it, not which one is bleeding most.
That choice is not right. The spurting wound is the loudest problem in the bay, so it pulls your hands first.
Haemorrhage is the commonest preventable death, but ask which problem would kill this man soonest if left alone.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: certainty about a bleed is how the loudest problem wins. Check what kills in minutes.

say.text: That choice is not right. Two IV lines feel like active resuscitation, and fluids are the first move most of us learn.
Lines and fluid matter soon, but the survey runs on the clock. Which problem would end this patient soonest?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: a familiar action is not the same as the first action.

say.text: The rule is time to death. Loss of airway kills faster than loss of breathing, which kills faster than loss of circulating blood volume.
Haemorrhage is the commonest preventable death, but that is a count, not an order. So the airway, with the neck held still, comes first.
Yes. The **airway** comes first, with the neck held still, in the fixed ABCDE order of the primary survey.
The order follows one rule: treat the greatest threat to life first. Losing airway kills faster than losing breathing, which kills faster than losing blood volume.

choices.label: Skip the lesson, I know the order

say.text: Haemorrhage is the commonest preventable death after injury. So which rule sets the order of the survey?

choices.label: Treat whichever problem kills fastest first
Treat the commonest cause of death first
Treat whichever bleeds most visibly first
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: A count tells you what is common across many patients. This survey runs on one patient, against the clock.
That choice is not right. A frequency list feels like a sensible ranking, because haemorrhage tops the count of preventable deaths.
A count describes a population. Which problem would end this patient soonest if left alone?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the rule: a common killer is not automatically the fastest one.

say.text: That choice is not right. Visible bleeding is the most dramatic problem, so it grabs attention before anything else.
Dramatic is not the same as fastest. Which problem ends this patient soonest, whatever is loudest in the room?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: the loudest problem and the fastest killer are often different.

say.text: A count is not an order. Haemorrhage is the commonest preventable death, but ABCDE is ordered by how fast each problem kills.
So the survey starts with A. Bleeding is controlled inside C, which comes after A and B.
Yes. ABCDE is a clock, so the problem that kills fastest is treated first.
Haemorrhage control sits inside C, the third step, so it is not moved to the front.

choices.label: Go deeper: the prehospital bleeding-first rule

say.text: Prehospital and military protocols, such as PHTLS and MARCH, put catastrophic bleeding control first, which some courses write as xABCDE.
For NEET PG the ATLS order is still ABCDE, with haemorrhage control inside C.
A different case. A man with a chest wound answers your questions clearly at the door.
What is the next step in the primary survey?

choices.label: Move on to the secondary survey
Check disability, he is clearly talking
Check breathing and ventilation right now
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Speech tells you about this moment. What does it not tell you about the lungs?
That choice is not right. A talking patient feels finished, so the rest of the survey starts to look like a formality.
Speech is only a snapshot for the moment. Which letter is still unchecked?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the qualifier: a talking patient has a patent airway for the moment, not for the rest of the survey.

say.text: That choice is not right. Clear speech looks like proof the brain is working, so a neuro check feels like the next box.
Speech does not show that air reaches the lungs. Which letter checks that?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: good speech tells you about the brain only after the airway and breathing are known.

say.text: Speech shows that, for the moment, the airway is patent and the brain is getting blood.
The next step is B: check that air actually reaches the lungs.
Yes. Talking shows the airway is open for the moment, so the next letter is B.
The next step is breathing, not intubation: check that air is reaching the lungs.
A classmate tells you: ATLS is built for the deaths that come days later in the ICU, from sepsis.
Which correction is right?

choices.label: ATLS aims at deaths in the first few hours
Agreed: it targets the sepsis deaths days later
The instant deaths at the scene are the target
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which deaths a team in the bay can still prevent, not which ones turn up weeks later.
Yes. The window ATLS is built for is the early period after injury, when prompt resuscitation most improves survival.
Deaths in that window are the **second peak**, minutes to several hours after injury.
That choice is not right. Late sepsis deaths are memorable, so the late window can feel like the course's job.
Sepsis and organ failure do kill, but they belong to a much later window, days to weeks after injury.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: the timing settles which peak you are looking at before the cause does.

say.text: That choice is not right. The instant deaths are the most dramatic, so they can feel like the first thing to target.
The **first peak** is seconds to minutes after injury, and only injury prevention reduces it. A survey cannot aim at that window.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: the fastest death is not always the one that can be changed.

say.text: Trauma deaths fall in three peaks. The first is seconds to minutes after injury, from brain, cord, heart or aortic injury.
The second is minutes to several hours after injury: subdural or epidural haematoma, haemopneumothorax, ruptured spleen, pelvic fracture. **ATLS targets this peak.**
The third is days to weeks later, from sepsis and multiple organ dysfunction.
Three problems in one trauma bay, none treated yet: a blocked airway, stopped breathing and heavy blood loss.
Put them in the order each would kill, fastest first.

choices.label: Blood loss, then airway, then breathing
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask how fast each problem stops oxygen reaching the brain, and how long blood loss takes to empty the vessels.
Yes. A blocked airway ends oxygen supply fastest, loss of breathing kills next, and loss of circulating blood volume comes last.
That is why the primary survey runs A, B, C, D, E in that fixed order.
That choice is not right. Blood is the visible threat, and blood loss sounds like the biggest killer on a trauma board.
Size of a threat is not the same as its clock. Ask which problem would stop this patient first.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: a large threat can still be a slow one.

say.text: That choice is not right. Blood loss is loud on the chart, so it can seem to outrank breathing.
Check which kills faster: a stopped breath, or the slower emptying of circulating blood volume.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: a loud problem can feel urgent without being the fastest killer.

say.text: Count the clock, not the chart. A blocked airway kills fastest, loss of breathing kills next, and loss of circulating blood volume takes longest.
Haemorrhage is the most common cause of preventable trauma death, but how large a threat is is not the same as how fast it kills.
So the survey runs airway, breathing, circulation, disability, exposure, in that order.
A 40-year-old is hit by a lorry and is brought into the bay.
Which of these deaths belongs to the second peak, minutes to hours after injury?

choices.label: Organ failure from sepsis, found on day ten
Ruptured aorta, dying within minutes of impact
Torn liver bleeding out in the first few hours
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Count the hours since the crash, not the days on the ward. Which death falls in that span?
Yes. A torn liver bleeding over the first hours is a second-peak death, minutes to several hours after injury.
That window is where prompt resuscitation most improves survival, which is why the survey is in a hurry.
That choice is not right. Organ failure on a ward is memorable, so it can feel like a trauma-course topic.
It is real, but it belongs to a much later window, days to weeks after injury.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: a death on day ten is a third-peak death, whatever its cause.

say.text: That choice is not right. A death at the scene is the most dramatic, so it can feel like the death a survey must answer.
A ruptured aorta is a real killer, but it belongs to the first peak, seconds to minutes after injury, which only prevention reduces.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: the earliest deaths are the ones a survey can least change.

say.text: The second peak is minutes to several hours after injury, with haematoma, haemopneumothorax, ruptured spleen, liver laceration and pelvic fracture.
It is the peak ATLS targets, because prompt resuscitation still changes the outcome in that window.
The first peak is seconds to minutes, and the third is days to weeks later, from sepsis.
So trauma deaths come in three peaks: the first at the scene, the second in the first hours, the third in the weeks after.
The primary survey comes first in the ATLS sequence, ahead of the secondary survey, and it runs in the order you just built.
Before we teach the airway, try a harder one. Make your call, and we will work through it after.

A 40-year-old cyclist was knocked off by a van. At the scene he spoke clearly to the crew. Now, in your bay, he is hoarse, with a swelling growing under his jaw and noisy breathing. What is your next move?

choices.label: Reassess the airway now, and prepare a definitive airway
He spoke clearly, so carry on with the survey
A hoarse voice only: analgesia, then the secondary survey
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what a swelling in the neck does to the airway over the next few minutes, not what he said at the scene.
Yes. A changing voice and a growing neck swelling mean the airway may close, so you reassess it at once and get ready for a definitive airway.
That choice is not right. Clear speech at the scene feels like proof the airway is fine, so the survey seems finished.
Speech showed the airway was open for the moment. The airway is changing now, and that is what you are deciding on.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the word moment. Speech is a snapshot, and a hoarse voice is one of the signs that the airway is changing.

say.text: That choice is not right. A hoarse voice sounds like a minor complaint, so treating the pain and moving on looks like the next job.
A changing voice with a swelling in the neck is one of the signs of airway compromise.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is worth a second look: a hoarse voice is an early airway sign, not a side complaint.

say.text: You picked to carry on. That reads the speech from the scene as if it still described the airway now.
Reassess the airway whenever the patient deteriorates. A neck haematoma can close the airway, so the airway decides the next step, not what he said earlier.
You picked analgesia and the secondary survey. That treats the voice and leaves the airway unchecked.
Look at the airway again now, and get ready for a definitive airway if it is failing.
The airway can change in minutes. Speech proves it was open at that moment, not that it will stay open.
Hoarseness, noisy breathing and a growing neck swelling are signs of compromise. A neck haematoma can obstruct the airway, which makes a definitive airway the indication.
A different patient. A man was talking at the scene. Now in the ambulance his GCS has fallen to 7 and he is not protecting his airway.
What decides the airway now?

choices.label: He moved his limbs earlier, so the airway is safe
GCS of 8 or less, which means he cannot protect it
Wait for a head CT before deciding on the tube
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Which measure in the stem is a score you can track, and what number does the rule use?
Yes. A GCS of 8 or less is the indication for a definitive airway, because the patient can no longer protect his own.
That choice is not right. Movement at the scene feels like a sign that the brain and airway are working, so the score seems less important.
Movement is a snapshot. The GCS is the measure that sets the airway trigger.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check what each finding measures: movement is an early sign, but the rule that decides the airway is the GCS.

say.text: You picked the reassuring movement. That turns one sign into an all-clear.
A GCS of 8 or less is an indication for a definitive airway, and a patient at that level cannot protect the airway.
Tempting, because a head scan feels like the thorough next step. The airway decision is made on the GCS, and imaging can follow it.
In an unconscious patient the airway most often fails because the tongue falls back against the pharynx. Snoring and gurgling are the warning signs.
Open the airway with a jaw thrust and keep the neck still, because the cervical spine is assumed injured. A definitive airway is a tube in the trachea with the cuff below the cords.
A 9-year-old was pulled from a house fire with burns to the face. Two intubation attempts have failed, and the saturation is falling.
Which emergency airway do you use?

choices.label: Surgical cricothyroidotomy, the usual adult emergency airway
Emergency tracheostomy, as a definitive surgical airway
Needle cricothyroidotomy with jet oxygenation for now
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think about the age in the stem: what does a child's cricoid cartilage need to stay intact?
Yes. Under 12, the emergency route is a needle, because the cricoid cartilage must not be cut in a child.
It is temporary: oxygenation lasts only about 30 to 45 minutes, so a definitive airway must follow.
That choice is not right. The adult rule feels like the safe default in a failed airway, and nothing in the stem flags a change.
The cricoid cartilage is the only complete ring supporting the upper trachea, and cutting it in a child risks lasting damage.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is the adult rule carried over without checking the age. Check the age before you choose.

say.text: Tempting, because a tracheostomy is a definitive airway and it sounds like a planned surgical route.
In an emergency it is slower and bleeds more than a cricothyroidotomy, so it is not the quick rescue this child needs.
You picked the adult surgical airway. The age in the stem changes the rule.
Adults get the surgical cricothyroidotomy. Under 12, the cricoid is the one ring to keep intact, so a needle is used.
Adults: surgical cricothyroidotomy is the emergency airway of choice, with the cut made through the cricothyroid membrane.
Under 12: avoid the surgical cut and use a needle cricothyroidotomy, which is temporary and gives oxygen for about 30 to 45 minutes.
The same failed airway, cannot intubate and cannot oxygenate, in two patients: a 35-year-old and a 9-year-old.
Which pair of emergency airways fits?

choices.label: Surgical cricothyroidotomy for both patients, to be safe
Needle cricothyroidotomy for both, since it is quicker
Surgical for the adult, needle for the child
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Take the two patients one at a time, and ask what the age changes about the cut.
Yes. The adult gets the surgical cricothyroidotomy, and the child gets the needle, because a child's cricoid cartilage must not be cut.
That choice is not right. One rule for both patients feels simpler and safer, and the adult surgical airway is the one you learned first.
The adult can take a surgical cut, but the cricoid ring of a child must not be cut.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is one rule for two patients. The age is the qualifier that splits them.

say.text: You picked one rule for both. The adult and the child differ at 12, so each gets its own airway.
The surgical cut is for adults; the needle is the child's temporary airway.
Tempting, because the needle is the quick rescue and seems to fit any failed airway.
A needle only bridges oxygen for a short time, and the adult still gets a surgical airway.
Two patients in the bay, both in shock, both with absent breath sounds on the right.
Tension pneumothorax or massive haemothorax? Which finding tells them apart?

choices.label: Absent breath sounds on the injured side
Muffled heart sounds with a falling pressure
Hyper-resonance on percussion, with distended neck veins
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Both sides are silent, so silence cannot separate them. Which bedside signs does air change, and which does blood change?
Air trapped under pressure makes the chest hyper-resonant and fills the neck veins. Blood dulls the percussion note.
The veins are often flat in blood loss from hypovolaemia, so percussion and neck veins are the discriminators, not breath sounds.
Yes. Air gives a hyper-resonant chest and distended neck veins; blood gives dullness, and its neck veins are often flat.
That choice is not right. Both patients are silent on that side, so silence feels like the sign that settles it.
Massive haemothorax is also silent on one side, so silence cannot separate the two.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the shared sign: silence on one side fits both.

say.text: That choice is not right. A falling pressure with a full neck feels like a heart-level problem, so the heart sounds seem to decide it.
Muffled heart sounds belong to the pericardium, and they do not separate air from blood in the chest.

sure_note.text: You were sure: muffled heart sounds point to the pericardium, not the pleura.

say.text: A stab wound to the right chest. He is hypotensive, his neck veins are distended, the right chest is hyper-resonant and breath sounds on that side are absent.
What is your next step?

choices.label: Portable chest X-ray first, then decide on treatment
Immediate needle decompression of the right chest
Intubate and ventilate with positive pressure
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Count what is in front of you: low pressure, a full neck and a silent side. Which step cannot wait for a film?
A one-way valve traps air in the pleural space; it collapses the lung and impedes venous return.
Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis, so decompress first, then tube and reassess, rather than wait for an X-ray.
Yes. Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis, and immediate needle decompression comes before anything else.
That choice is not right. A film feels like the careful step before any procedure, and that habit is strong.
A film can wait only while the patient is stable, and this one is in shock.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the habit: imaging first is the trap in shock.

say.text: That choice is not right. Airway is the first letter, so a tube feels like the first move.
Positive pressure only adds air to a space that already has a one-way leak, so the chest is the problem first.

sure_note.text: You were sure: a secure airway does not treat the leak that is filling the chest.

say.text: Picture an untreated tension pneumothorax, with air already trapped by a one-way valve.
You now push positive-pressure breaths in. What happens to the pressure in that space?

choices.label: It pushes more air into the trapped space, raising pressure
It re-expands the collapsed lung and relieves the shift
It pulls the mediastinum toward the collapsed lung
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Air that enters the pleural space through the leak has no way out. Ask what another breath does to that trapped air.
The valve lets air in and not out, so pleural pressure rises with every breath.
Rising pressure shifts the mediastinum to the other side and impedes venous return, so it must be relieved first.
Yes. Trapped air under rising pressure pushes the mediastinum and cuts venous return.
That choice is not right. Re-inflating a collapsed lung is what a breath is meant to do, so the picture feels right.
Here the valve lets air in and not out. Ask what a breath does to a space the valve keeps filling.

sure_note.text: You were sure: a one-way leak fills the space; it does not drain it.

say.text: That choice is not right. A collapsed lung looks like it should drag things toward it, so the pull feels plausible.
Ask what is doing the pushing here: the collapsed lung, or the air under pressure.

sure_note.text: You were sure: the trapped air is pushing, not the lung pulling.

say.text: In the primary survey, what confirms a tension pneumothorax?

choices.label: Upright chest X-ray showing a shifted mediastinum
Bedside clinical findings on examination of the chest
CT chest before treatment, to see the pleura
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: The primary survey runs on what kills in minutes. Which of these can be found at the bedside, without a machine?
The diagnosis is clinical: unilateral absent breath sounds, hyper-resonance, distended neck veins and shock.
The physiology kills while you wait, so the bedside signs decide the step, and imaging follows only once the patient is stable.
Yes. The diagnosis is clinical, and a film is not needed before treatment.
That choice is not right. A film is what most exam stems pair with a chest diagnosis, so the X-ray feels like the confirmation.
A film can wait only while the patient is stable. The primary survey runs on what kills in minutes, and a film takes longer.

sure_note.text: You were sure: a film is the habit, not the primary survey's test.

say.text: That choice is not right. CT is the thorough test in trauma, so it feels like the complete answer.
Thorough is not the same as first; the primary survey is built on what can be done at the bedside.

sure_note.text: You were sure: a thorough scan is not the first test in the primary survey.

say.text: ATLS 10th edition: where is needle decompression placed in an adult?

choices.label: 2nd intercostal space, in the mid-clavicular line
3rd intercostal space, at the anterior axillary line
4th or 5th intercostal space, anterior to the mid-axillary line
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Two editions give two answers. Which one is the current adult site, and why would chest wall thickness matter?
ATLS 10th edition places the adult site in the 4th or 5th intercostal space, just anterior to the mid-axillary line.
A catheter at the old site can be too short to reach the pleura through a thick adult chest wall.
Yes. The adult site is the 4th or 5th space, anterior to the mid-axillary line, where a catheter can reach the pleura.
That choice is not right. It is the site most older books and past keys give, so it feels like the standard answer.
That site is the child's ATLS site, and the adult site has moved since, so the edition matters here.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so hold both keys: old and current editions differ on the adult site.

say.text: That choice is not right. It sits close to the right area, so a half-remembered site picks it up.
Near-misses lose the exact interspace and line that ATLS names, so check both the space and the line.

sure_note.text: You were sure, but the exact space and line are what the exam tests.

say.text: A 6-year-old has a tension pneumothorax with the same signs as an adult.
Where do you place the needle now?

choices.label: 4th or 5th space, just anterior to mid-axillary line
2nd intercostal space, at the mid-clavicular line
Chest X-ray to choose the site before needling
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: The age in the stem matters. Which site does the child keep, and which did the adult edition change?
ATLS keeps the 2nd intercostal space at the mid-clavicular line for children, while the adult site moved.
A child's thinner chest wall lets a short catheter still reach the pleura at that site.
Yes. In a child the site is the 2nd intercostal space at the mid-clavicular line; the adult site is for adults.
That choice is not right. You learned the current adult site most recently, so it is the one that comes to mind.
The adult site does not carry over to a child; ATLS keeps a different site by age.

sure_note.text: You were sure: the site follows age and edition, not the most recent memory.

say.text: That choice is not right. A film feels safe before any procedure, even in a child.
Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis at any age, and a film does not choose the site.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the habit: imaging first is the trap in this condition.

say.text: On the right, the lung keeps collapsing and the trapped air keeps pushing.
Which way does the mediastinum move?

choices.label: It is pulled toward the collapsed right lung
It is pushed to the left, impeding venous return
It shifts right, toward the injured side with the lung
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what is doing the pushing: the collapsed lung, or the air trapped under pressure? Then ask which way that push goes.
Rising pleural pressure pushes the mediastinum to the opposite side and impedes venous return.
So the trachea moves away from the injured side, and the neck veins fill.
Yes. Trapped air under rising pressure pushes the mediastinum across and impedes venous return.
That choice is not right. A collapsed lung looks like it should drag its neighbours in with it.
The force here is air under rising pressure, not the lung's pull.

sure_note.text: You were sure: pressure pushes, and the collapsed lung does not drag.

say.text: That choice is not right. Shifting toward the injured side is what a collapsed lung seems to do on a picture.
The direction is set by the pressure, not by the side of the injury. Check which way the trachea moves.

sure_note.text: You were sure: check the direction, because it is the detail the exam tests.

say.text: A right-sided tension pneumothorax, examined at the bedside.
Which pair of findings do you expect?

choices.label: Trachea deviated to the left, hyper-resonance on the right
Trachea deviated to the right, hyper-resonance on the right
Trachea central, with dullness to percussion on the right
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think about where the pressure pushes the trachea, and which percussion note trapped air gives.
Trapped air under pressure pushes the trachea to the opposite side and leaves the injured chest hyper-resonant.
The same pressure impedes venous return, which is why the neck veins fill.
Yes. Hyper-resonance on the injured side, with the trachea pushed to the other side, is the expected pair.
That choice is not right. The trachea tracks the injured side in many pictures, so it feels like the same side.

That choice is not right. Dullness is the sign of blood, so a dull right chest feels like it belongs to this picture.

A man has three ribs each broken in two places, and a segment of chest wall moves paradoxically. His saturation is falling.
What is the main cause of his hypoxia?

choices.label: Paradoxical movement of the flail segment
Underlying pulmonary contusion of the lung beneath
An associated open pneumothorax from the same injury
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: The moving segment is what you can see. Ask what the lung under it is doing to the blood's oxygen.
A flail segment is two or more adjacent ribs, each fractured in two or more places.
The hypoxia comes from the contusion underneath; the paradoxical movement is only the visible sign.
Yes. The contusion causes the hypoxia; the paradoxical movement is only its sign.
That choice is not right. The moving segment is the visible injury, so it is easy to take for the cause.

sure_note.text: You were sure: a sign you can see is not the same as the cause.

say.text: That choice is not right. Any chest injury on the list feels like a candidate for the hypoxia.

sure_note.text: You were sure: a listed injury is not automatically the cause.

say.text: Flail chest with a bruised lung on the monitor, and his saturation is still falling.
Which management treats the cause?

choices.label: Urgent surgical fixation of the loose segment

Intubation fails and oxygen cannot be delivered in two patients: a 9-year-old and a 30-year-old. Which emergency surgical airway for each?

choices.label: Surgical cricothyroidotomy for the adult, needle for the child
Needle cricothyroidotomy for both, as the safer route
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Right. Adults get the surgical route; under about 12 years a needle route is used.
The answer: surgical cricothyroidotomy for the 30-year-old, needle cricothyroidotomy for the 9-year-old. The cutoff is about 12 years, because the cricoid is at risk in children.
That choice is not right.
The bleeding is the loudest problem, so it feels first. But the order follows speed of death, and haemorrhage control sits inside C. Airway and breathing come before circulation in the ATLS order.
That choice is not right.

He is speaking, so it feels like he is stable. But talking shows an open airway only for the moment, and his breathing is poor. Short phrases and fast shallow breaths mean breathing needs attention now.
A cyclist hit by a van talks in short phrases. His thigh is bleeding steadily and his breathing is fast and shallow. What do you do first?

choices.label: Put a tourniquet on the thigh, since bleeding kills most
Move on to the secondary survey, since he is talking
Reassess airway and breathing now, and treat problems before the bleed

say.text: Right. Talking in short phrases with fast shallow breathing needs B dealt with first; the bleed is handled in C.
The answer: reassess airway and breathing first, then control the bleed under C. The order follows what kills fastest, and talking only shows the airway for the moment.
That choice is not right.

Two litres is the figure older keys print, so it feels standard. ATLS 10th edition gives 1 L warmed, with early blood. The current adult bolus is 1 L warmed isotonic crystalloid; large volumes dilute clotting and cool the patient.
That choice is not right.
Eight hours sticks in memory as the limit, so waiting feels safe. But 8 hours is the infusion; the start window is 3 hours. He is at 2 hours, inside the window. Waiting risks missing it.
An adult weighing 70 kg arrives 2 hours after a crash with a bleeding pelvis and BP 80/50. Which initial plan is right?

choices.label: 2 L crystalloid fast, then blood if there is no response
1 L warmed crystalloid, early blood, TXA now
Hold TXA until CT, as it works up to 8 hours

say.text: Right. This is the 10th edition bolus, early blood, and TXA still inside its 3-hour window.
The answer: 1 L warmed crystalloid, early blood, and TXA now. Exam note: older keys print 2 L. TXA starts within 3 hours of injury; the 8 hours is the second infusion.
That choice is not right.
He cannot pass urine, so a catheter feels like the obvious relief. But these signs suggest a urethral tear. A catheter is held back until a urethrogram shows an intact urethra.
That choice is not right.
CT is the thorough test, so it feels careful. But an unstable patient should not go to the scanner. Use the bedside test in the room; imaging waits for stability.
A cyclist falls astride the bar. He has perineal bruising and a high-riding prostate, cannot pass urine, and has an unstable pelvis with BP 85. What comes before any catheter?

choices.label: A Foley catheter now, to relieve the retention and measure urine
CT of the abdomen and pelvis, to map the injury
A retrograde urethrogram to check the urethra

say.text: Right. The urethra is checked first, and the catheter goes in only if it is intact.
The answer: a retrograde urethrogram first. Perineal bruising and a high-riding prostate suggest a torn urethra, and the catheter must wait.
That choice is not right.

The moving segment is the visible problem, so fixing it feels like treating the cause. But it is the sign, not the cause. The hypoxia comes from the lung beneath the segment, so treatment goes to the lung.
That choice is not right.
Rib fractures often bring a pneumothorax, so it feels likely. But the main cause here is the contusion beneath the segment. The contusion drives the low oxygen, not a simple pneumothorax.
An older man falls and breaks three ribs on the right, each in two places. A segment moves paradoxically and his saturation is 88%. Which statement is right?

choices.label: Fixing the moving segment will correct the hypoxia
A small simple pneumothorax is the main cause of the hypoxia
The bruised lung is the cause; oxygen, analgesia, ventilate if needed

say.text: Right. The pulmonary contusion causes the hypoxia, so treatment targets the lung.
The answer: the underlying pulmonary contusion is the main cause. The paradoxical movement marks the injury, and treatment goes to the lung.
That choice is not right.

Permissive hypotension is a real strategy for bleeding, so it seems right for her. But it is not used with a brain injury. The injured brain needs perfusion; secondary brain injury follows low pressure and low oxygen.
That choice is not right.

Pushing fluid is the reflex for a low pressure, and 2 L is the older figure. But large volumes worsen bleeding, and the 10th edition bolus is 1 L. Use a smaller warmed bolus with early blood while keeping the brain perfused.
A woman with a bleeding spleen also has a head injury, GCS 7, and a systolic BP of 85. The surgeon wants to run the pressure low until theatre. What is right?

choices.label: Agree, because a low pressure protects the clot in any bleeding patient
Give 2 L crystalloid fast to bring the pressure up
Keep pressure high enough to perfuse the brain; find the bleeding

say.text: Right. Permissive hypotension is not used in brain injury, so the brain is kept perfused.
The answer: keep perfusion adequate for the brain and control the bleeding. Permissive hypotension is not used in traumatic brain injury.
That choice is not right.
Normal numbers are reassuring, so shock feels excluded. But beta-blockers and age blunt the heart-rate response. Tachycardia can be absent, so pale cool skin and confusion are signs to act on.
That choice is not right.
Class II seems like it should already lower the pressure. But hypotension first appears in Class III. A normal BP does not exclude shock; compensation holds the pressure.
A 72-year-old on a beta-blocker falls. Pulse 78, BP 118/76, skin cool and pale, and he is confused. How do you read this?

choices.label: No shock, since the pulse and BP are both normal
Early shock only, since hypotension would already show by Class II
Shock may be present, since drugs and age blunt the usual signs

say.text: Right. Pale cool skin and confusion are warnings when tachycardia is blunted.
The answer: shock may be present. Beta-blockers and age can hide tachycardia, and hypotension appears late, in Class III, so act on the skin and mental state.
That choice is not right.

Low pressure with full neck veins looks like a pressure problem in the pleura. But tension pneumothorax gives a silent, hyper-resonant side and a deviated trachea. Here the breath sounds are equal and the trachea is central.
That choice is not right.
A chest wound with shock makes blood loss the first thought. But haemothorax gives a dull, silent side, and both sides are clear here. Look for one-sided dullness; there is none.
That choice is not right.

A collapsed lung looks like it should drag things toward it. But a collapsed lung does not give this picture, and in tension the mediastinum is pushed away. The findings here point to the heart, not a pleural collapse.
A man is shot in the left chest. BP 70, neck veins distended, heart sounds faint, trachea central, and breath sounds clear and equal. What is the likely diagnosis?

choices.label: Tension pneumothorax, since low BP and full neck veins fit
Massive haemothorax, since shock after a chest wound means blood
Cardiac tamponade, with blood around the heart
A collapsed lung, which pulls the mediastinum toward the injured side

say.text: Right. Hypotension, muffled heart sounds and distended neck veins with clear lungs is Beck's triad.
The answer: cardiac tamponade. Beck's triad with clear, equal breath sounds and a central trachea points to the pericardium, not the pleura.

K2.text: Primary survey order: **A**irway with restriction of cervical spine motion, **B**reathing and ventilation, **C**irculation with haemorrhage control, **D**isability (neurological status), **E**xposure and environmental control.

K3.text: The order follows the principle **"treat the greatest threat to life first"**: loss of airway kills faster than loss of breathing, which kills faster than loss of circulating blood volume.

K4.text: A patient who **talks normally** has, for the moment, a patent airway, adequate breathing and adequate cerebral perfusion.

K5.text: A **GCS of 8 or less** is an indication for a **definitive airway**.

K6.text: **Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis**; treat it with immediate decompression and **do not wait for a chest X-ray**.

K7.text: **Haemorrhage** is the leading cause of preventable death after injury, and hypotension in a trauma patient is treated as **hypovolaemic (haemorrhagic) shock until proven otherwise**.

K8.text: In haemorrhagic shock, **hypotension first appears in Class III** (31–40% blood volume loss).

K9.text: Initial fluid bolus in ATLS 10th edition: **1 L warmed isotonic crystalloid in adults, 20 mL/kg in children**.

K10.text: **Surgical cricothyroidotomy** is the preferred emergency surgical airway in adults and is avoided in children under about 12 years, in whom **needle cricothyroidotomy** is used.

K11.text: The **secondary survey** (head-to-toe examination with **AMPLE** history) starts only after the primary survey is complete and resuscitation is under way.

K15.text: The **"golden hour"** is the early period after injury during which prompt resuscitation most improves survival; ATLS is aimed at deaths occurring in this period.

K16.text: ATLS sequence of initial assessment: preparation → triage → **primary survey (ABCDE)** with simultaneous resuscitation → adjuncts to primary survey → consider need for patient transfer → **secondary survey** → adjuncts to secondary survey → continued post-resuscitation monitoring and re-evaluation → definitive care.

K18.text: **First peak**: seconds to minutes after injury (e.g. severe brain or high spinal cord injury, rupture of heart or aorta); reduced only by **injury prevention**.

K19.text: **Second peak**: minutes to several hours after injury (e.g. subdural/epidural haematoma, haemopneumothorax, ruptured spleen, liver laceration, pelvic fracture, multiple injuries with major blood loss); this is the peak **ATLS targets**.

K20.text: **Third peak**: days to weeks after injury, from **sepsis and multiple organ dysfunction**.

K23.text: The most common cause of airway obstruction in an unconscious patient is the **tongue falling back** against the posterior pharynx.

K24.text: In tension pneumothorax, a one-way valve air leak traps air in the pleural space, collapsing the lung, shifting the mediastinum to the opposite side and **impeding venous return**, causing obstructive shock.

K26.text: In **flail chest**, the main cause of hypoxia is the **underlying pulmonary contusion**, not the paradoxical chest-wall movement itself.

K29.text: **Neurogenic shock** from spinal cord injury causes hypotension **with bradycardia** (loss of sympathetic tone), unlike haemorrhagic shock, which causes tachycardia.

K31.text: Signs of airway compromise: agitation, obtundation, cyanosis, use of accessory muscles, **noisy breathing (snoring, gurgling, stridor)**, hoarseness and tracheal deviation.

K32.text: Assume a **cervical spine injury** in every patient with multisystem blunt trauma, especially with altered consciousness or blunt injury above the clavicle.

K33.text: Life-threatening chest injuries to identify in the primary survey: **tension pneumothorax, open pneumothorax, massive haemothorax, flail chest with pulmonary contusion, and cardiac tamponade** (the last assessed with circulation).

K34.text: **Tension pneumothorax**: respiratory distress, tachycardia, hypotension, **tracheal deviation away** from the affected side, unilateral absent breath sounds, **hyper-resonance**, distended neck veins and, late, cyanosis.

K35.text: **Massive haemothorax**: shock with absent breath sounds and **dullness to percussion** on one side; neck veins may be flat from hypovolaemia.

K36.text: **Flail chest**: two or more adjacent ribs each fractured in **two or more places**, producing a segment with **paradoxical movement**.

K37.text: Key bedside indicators of perfusion: **level of consciousness, skin colour, and pulse** (rate and character).

K39.text: **Cardiac tamponade**: **Beck's triad** = hypotension, **muffled heart sounds** and **distended neck veins**.

K41.text: **Narrowed pulse pressure** (Class II) is an early sign of haemorrhage, appearing before systolic BP falls.

K43.text: Tachycardia may be absent in the elderly, athletes, patients on **beta-blockers** and those with pacemakers.

K44.text: In children, **hypotension is a late sign** of shock because of their large physiological reserve.

K50.text: **Urinary catheter** to monitor urine output; it is **contraindicated** when urethral injury is suspected — **blood at the urethral meatus**, perineal ecchymosis or a **high-riding prostate** — until a **retrograde urethrogram** confirms an intact urethra.

K53.text: **FAST** (Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma) looks for free fluid in four windows: **pericardial (subxiphoid), right upper quadrant (hepatorenal / Morison's pouch), left upper quadrant (splenorenal) and pelvis (suprapubic)**.

K56.text: Imaging and adjuncts must **not delay resuscitation** or transfer; a haemodynamically unstable patient should not go to the CT scanner.

K58.text: Basic manoeuvres: **chin lift** or **jaw thrust** (jaw thrust preferred when cervical spine injury is possible), suction, and **oropharyngeal or nasopharyngeal airway**.

K63.text: A **definitive airway** is a tube placed **in the trachea with the cuff inflated below the vocal cords**, connected to oxygen-enriched assisted ventilation and secured in place.

K65.text: Indications for a definitive airway: inability to maintain or protect the airway (e.g. **GCS ≤8**, severe maxillofacial fractures, risk of aspiration, risk of obstruction from neck haematoma, laryngeal or tracheal injury, **inhalation burns**), inability to maintain oxygenation or ventilation, and apnoea.

K67.text: When intubation fails and the airway cannot be maintained, a **surgical airway** is indicated; **surgical cricothyroidotomy** is preferred to emergency tracheostomy because it is faster, easier and bleeds less.

K68.text: **Needle cricothyroidotomy** with jet insufflation is a temporary measure; adequate oxygenation lasts only about **30–45 minutes** because CO2 accumulates.

K69.text: Surgical cricothyroidotomy is not recommended in children **under 12 years** because of the risk of damage to the **cricoid cartilage**, the only circumferential support of the upper trachea.

K72.text: **Tension pneumothorax**: immediate **needle decompression** followed by **tube thoracostomy**.

K73.text: ATLS 10th edition site for needle decompression in **adults**: **4th or 5th intercostal space just anterior to the mid-axillary line**.

K74.text: ATLS 10th edition site for needle decompression in **children**: **2nd intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line**.

K81.text: **Flail chest with pulmonary contusion**: oxygen, adequate **analgesia**, judicious fluids, and ventilation (intubation) if hypoxia persists.

K83.text: Venous access: **two large-calibre (at least 18-gauge) peripheral IV catheters**.

K84.text: If peripheral access fails, use **intraosseous** access or a central/venous cut-down line.

K86.text: Fluids are **warmed to about 39 °C** to prevent hypothermia.

K87.text: Initial fluid in ATLS 10th edition: **1 L isotonic crystalloid in adults, 20 mL/kg in children under 40 kg**, then **blood products** early.

K88.text: **Balanced resuscitation / permissive hypotension**: accept a lower-than-normal BP until bleeding is controlled to avoid "popping the clot", **not** used in traumatic brain injury.

K92.text: **Tranexamic acid** is given **within 3 hours of injury**: **1 g IV over 10 minutes, then 1 g over 8 hours** (CRASH-2).

K94.text: **Pelvic fracture** bleeding: apply a **pelvic binder (or sheet) centred over the greater trochanters**.

K97.text: Prevent **secondary brain injury** by maintaining adequate **oxygenation and perfusion**.

K100.text: **Reassess the primary survey (ABCDE) whenever the patient deteriorates**.

K102.text: **Secondary survey**: complete head-to-toe examination and **AMPLE** history — **A**llergies, **M**edications, **P**ast illnesses / **P**regnancy, **L**ast meal, **E**vents / **E**nvironment related to injury.

K106.text: Pregnant patients can lose **up to about 30–35% of blood volume** before showing signs of shock, because of physiological hypervolaemia.

K107.text: **Elderly**: limited physiological reserve; normal vital signs may hide shock.

K111.text: Iatrogenic hypothermia, dilutional coagulopathy and **abdominal compartment syndrome** from excessive crystalloid infusion.

K112.text: Needle decompression may fail when the catheter is **too short to reach the pleural space** in a thick chest wall, which is why ATLS moved the adult site to the 4th/5th ICS.

K116.text: Most common cause of preventable trauma death — **Haemorrhage**

K117.text: Most common cause of shock in trauma — **Hypovolaemic (haemorrhagic)**

K119.text: Emergency surgical airway of choice (adult) — **Surgical cricothyroidotomy**

K120.text: Surgical airway in child <12 years — **Needle cricothyroidotomy**

K121.text: Initial bedside test for intra-abdominal bleeding in unstable patient — **FAST**

K122.text: Investigation of choice for suspected urethral injury before catheterisation — **Retrograde urethrogram**

K123.text: First sign of shock to appear as BP still normal — **Tachycardia / narrowed pulse pressure**

K124.text: Class in which hypotension first appears — **Class III** (31–40%)

K126.text: Antifibrinolytic in bleeding trauma — **Tranexamic acid** within 3 h

K128.text: **Needle decompression site**: PYQs and older texts have expected the **2nd intercostal space, mid-clavicular line**; ATLS 10th edition places it at the **4th/5th ICS just anterior to the mid-axillary line in adults** and keeps the 2nd ICS MCL for children.

K129.text: **Initial fluid volume**: older ATLS editions and PYQ keys expected **2 L crystalloid in adults**; ATLS 10th edition reduced it to **1 L**, with early blood products.

K133.text: **C before A (xABCDE / <C>ABCDE)**: military and prehospital protocols (e.g. PHTLS, MARCH) put **catastrophic external haemorrhage control first**; for NEET PG the expected ATLS order remains **ABCDE**, with haemorrhage control inside C

K136.text: The **"talking patient"** question: a patient who answers clearly has a patent airway for now — the next step is **B** (breathing), not intubation.

K137.text: Trap: in an unstable patient, **CT abdomen is wrong**; the expected answer is **FAST** (or DPL) in the resuscitation room.

cards.q: What sets the order of the primary survey?
cards.a: Speed of death: airway in minutes, then breathing, then circulation with haemorrhage control.

cards.q: What does a patient who talks normally show?
cards.a: A patent airway, breathing and cerebral perfusion for the moment; the next step is breathing, not intubation.

cards.q: Emergency surgical airway: adult versus a child under 12?
cards.a: Surgical cricothyroidotomy in adults; needle cricothyroidotomy under about 12, since the cricoid can be damaged.

cards.q: When and where is tension pneumothorax decompressed?
cards.a: At once, on clinical diagnosis; in adults at the 4th or 5th intercostal space, anterior to the mid-axillary line.

cards.q: How do tension pneumothorax, massive haemothorax and tamponade differ?
cards.a: Tension: hyper-resonance, trachea away, distended neck veins. Haemothorax: dullness, flat neck veins. Tamponade: muffled heart sounds, Beck's triad.

cards.q: Where does hypotension first appear in haemorrhagic shock?
cards.a: Class III, 31 to 40 percent loss. Neurogenic shock gives hypotension with bradycardia; normal vitals mislead in the elderly and beta-blocked.

cards.q: Initial adult crystalloid, and the brain-injury target?
cards.a: 1 L warmed isotonic crystalloid in ATLS 10th edition, where the older key gave 2 L; permissive hypotension is not used in brain injury.

cards.q: Unstable patient: CT or FAST? And before a catheter in urethral injury?
cards.a: FAST in the resuscitation room; a retrograde urethrogram before any catheter.

cards.q: Which antifibrinolytic, and within what time?
cards.a: Tranexamic acid within 3 hours of injury: 1 g over 10 minutes, then 1 g over 8 hours.

avoided.text: You read the pulse and skin, not only the pressure.

fell_recovered.text: You first called low pressure after trauma haemorrhagic, then changed. A slow pulse with warm dry skin points to neurogenic shock, while haemorrhage gives tachycardia. Hypovolaemia stays the default only until the pulse says otherwise.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected on the spot, but not on a fresh question. Your model stops at hypotension and calls it blood loss. Neurogenic shock gives hypotension with bradycardia and warm skin. Use the side-by-side contrast on the O6 review card.

avoided.text: You used percussion and neck veins to separate air from blood.

fell_recovered.text: You first treated tension pneumothorax and massive haemothorax as one picture, then changed. Both have absent breath sounds, so that finding separates nothing; hyper-resonance with full neck veins is air, dullness with flat veins is blood.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected on the spot, but not on a fresh question. Your model treats any silent unilateral chest as one problem. Percuss and read the neck veins. Revisit the contrast on the O5 review card.

avoided.text: You kept tamponade apart from tension pneumothorax using heart and breath sounds.

fell_recovered.text: You first gave Beck's triad to tension pneumothorax, then changed. Beck's triad is hypotension, muffled heart sounds and distended neck veins; tamponade has clear breath sounds. Raised neck veins alone are shared.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected on the spot, but not on a fresh question. Your model stops at hypotension with raised neck veins. Check the heart sounds and the breath sounds. See the tamponade versus tension table on the O5 review card.

avoided.text: You knew blood pressure is a late sign of haemorrhage.

fell_recovered.text: You first expected low BP early, then changed. Compensation holds systolic pressure until about a third of blood is lost, so hypotension first appears in Class III. Tachycardia and narrow pulse pressure come first.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected on the spot, but not on a fresh question. Your model assumes BP falls as soon as loss is moderate. Anchor to compensation: hypotension first appears in Class III, 31 to 40 percent. Revisit the O6 review card.

avoided.text: You gave the current fluid figure and knew why it changed.

fell_recovered.text: You first answered the older 2 L key, then changed. ATLS 10th edition says 1 L warmed isotonic crystalloid, then early blood, because large volumes dilute clotting factors and cool the patient. Both keys exist, so read which edition the question follows.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected on the spot, but not on a fresh question. Your model retrieves the number printed in older books. Old keys say 2 L; ATLS 10th edition says 1 L plus early blood. Note both on the O7 review card.

avoided.text: You gave the adult and child decompression sites correctly.

fell_recovered.text: You first gave the older 2nd space mid-clavicular site for an adult, then changed. ATLS 10th edition uses the 4th or 5th space just in front of the mid-axillary line in adults and keeps the 2nd space for children. Be ready for either key.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected on the spot, but not on a fresh question. Your model holds the older memorised site without tying it to age or edition. PYQs expect the 2nd space; ATLS 10th edition uses the 4th or 5th for adults. Write both on the O4 review card.

avoided.text: You linked flail chest hypoxia to the contusion, not the moving segment.

fell_recovered.text: You first blamed the paradoxical movement for the hypoxia, then changed. The visible sign defines the injury, but the underlying pulmonary contusion causes the hypoxia, so treatment is oxygen, analgesia and cautious fluids.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected on the spot, but not on a fresh question. Your model takes the sign for the cause, so you would treat the movement, not the lung. The contusion drives the hypoxia. See the flail chest part of the O5 review card.

avoided.text: You pictured pressure pushing the mediastinum away from the tension side.

fell_recovered.text: You first reversed the shift, then changed. Trapped air under pressure pushes the mediastinum and trachea to the opposite side and kinks the great veins; a collapsed lung does not pull them over.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected on the spot, but not on a fresh question. Your model pictures the collapse pulling the trachea toward the injured side. Trace the valve, rising pressure, push to the opposite side. Redo the mechanism on the O5 review card.

avoided.text: You doubted normal vitals in the groups that blunt them.

fell_recovered.text: You first trusted normal vital signs in a qualifier patient, then changed. Beta-blockers and age blunt the pulse, children hold pressure until late, and pregnancy hides up to about a third of blood volume. Check the qualifier first.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected on the spot, but not on a fresh question. Your model uses normal vitals as default reassurance. Check age, pregnancy and drugs every time before accepting them. Compare the two patients on the O6 review card.

avoided.text: You checked age before choosing a surgical airway.

fell_recovered.text: You first used the adult surgical airway in a child, then changed. Under about 12 years use needle cricothyroidotomy, because the cricoid is the only complete ring and is easily damaged. Check age whenever a surgical airway is on the table.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected on the spot, but not on a fresh question. Your model applies the adult rule to a child. Ask the age: adult surgical, child under 12 needle cricothyroidotomy. See the O3 review card.

avoided.text: You looked for urethral injury signs before catheterising.

fell_recovered.text: You first catheterised in a patient with possible urethral injury, then changed. Blood at the meatus or a high-riding prostate means a retrograde urethrogram first. The routine catheter is the habit to watch.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected on the spot, but not on a fresh question. Your model treats the catheter as automatic. Scan for meatal blood, perineal bruising and a high prostate, then urethrogram, then catheter. See the O8 review card.

avoided.text: You matched ATLS to the second peak of trauma deaths.

fell_recovered.text: You first linked ATLS to the third peak, then changed. ATLS targets the second peak, minutes to hours after injury, where resuscitation can change the outcome; sepsis and organ failure are the third.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected on the spot, but not on a fresh question. Your model links the most familiar late cause of death to ATLS. Pair each peak with what can change it. See the O11 review card.

avoided.text: You held the five life-threatening chest injuries, tamponade included.

fell_recovered.text: You first built the chest list loosely, then changed. The five are tension pneumothorax, open pneumothorax, massive haemothorax, flail chest with contusion, and tamponade assessed under circulation. Simple pneumothorax is not one of them.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected on the spot, but not on a fresh question. Your model stores chest injuries as a vague pile and drops tamponade. Rebuild the five from oxygenation, ventilation and filling. See the O5 review card.

avoided.text: You checked for a head injury before accepting low pressure.

fell_recovered.text: You first applied permissive hypotension in a head-injured patient, then changed. It is not used in traumatic brain injury, where the brain needs adequate perfusion. Check for a head injury first.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected on the spot, but not on a fresh question. Your model applies the haemorrhage rule to everyone. Ask whether the brain needs a higher perfusion pressure. See the O7 review card.

avoided.text: You separated the 3-hour window from the 8-hour infusion.

fell_recovered.text: You first gave tranexamic acid on the 8-hour figure, then changed. Start within 3 hours of injury; 1 g over 10 minutes then 1 g over 8 hours is the regimen, and 8 is its duration, not its window.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected on the spot, but not on a fresh question. Your model files the memorable number under the wrong label. The window is 3 hours; the infusion is 8. See the O10 review card.

E1.text: You tend to merge look-alikes: shared findings such as absent breath sounds or low pressure feel like one picture. Before naming a diagnosis, find the one sign that only one condition has (percussion, neck veins, pulse, heart sounds).

E2.text: You tend to build lists loosely, adding familiar items or dropping the odd one out. Rebuild a set from its logic, then test it with 'which is NOT'.

E3.text: You tend to reverse direction or cause: sign for cause, collapse for pressure. Predict what happens step by step from the mechanism before choosing.

E4.text: You tend to stretch a reassuring sign beyond its qualifier. Reread the exact words, such as 'for the moment', and ask when the sign could fail.

E5.text: You tend to answer with the older exam key. Learn both: what PYQs expected and what ATLS 10th edition says, with the reason for the change.

E6.text: You tend to swap numbers, attaching a figure to the wrong label such as window versus infusion or class versus percentage. Anchor each number to what it means, then retest it in a case.

E7.text: You tend to drop the qualifier: age, drug, pregnancy or brain injury. Before using a rule, ask who this patient is and whether the rule has an exception.

E8.text: You tend to pick the test or step by accuracy or routine, not by stability and warning signs. Ask first whether this patient can afford the delay and whether a sign forbids the routine.

E9.text: You tend to get priorities wrong, choosing by what is visible, common or the first letter. Order by time to death and by physiology, then decide.

E10.text: You tend to attach a fact to the nearest familiar item, such as sepsis to ATLS. Pair each item with its own example and what can change it.

overconfident.text: You tapped Sure on two or more answers that were wrong. Those are the most useful errors, since a confident error corrected is remembered well. Do their review cards first, and before tapping Sure, name the qualifier or discriminating sign that makes you certain.

underconfident.text: You tapped Guessing on several answers you got right. Your knowledge is ahead of your confidence. Next time, say the reason before you tap, and if it holds, tap Sure.

calibrated.text: Your confidence tracked your accuracy: Sure answers were mostly right and doubt appeared where you missed. That is a useful exam skill, so keep tagging answers honestly.

hints_heavy.text: You asked for hints or explanations often. That is fine while learning, but unaided recall is what the exam tests. Revisit the cards for the objectives where you asked, and answer first before opening help.

hints_none.text: You asked for no hints, so your misses were real recall gaps rather than missing information. Use the review cards to refill those, then retest without help.

hinted_only.text: On some objectives you were right only after a hint. Treat those as not yet secure: redo their review cards and answer cold before opening any help.

fast_lane.text: You skipped at least one lesson, such as the ABCDE order, the peaks recap, the worked shock cases or the management plan, and went straight to the questions. Skipping is a fair call, but it does not show mastery. Review the cards for those skipped lessons.

gap.text: Start with the review cards for objectives marked gap, and confident errors first. Do one card per sitting, say the discriminating feature or qualifier aloud, then retest on a fresh question. Revisit the fell-open items after a day.

clear.text: No objective is a gap. Space the review cards over the next days and weeks, and rehearse both keys for the old-versus-ATLS 10th edition items so they hold under exam pressure.
